## QUESTION 1

Cap Anson and Nolan Ryan had the longest careers in the data, each playing 27 seasons. All ten players in the results played between 25 and 27 seasons. I counted the different years each player appeared in a game, so changing teams during a season did not count as an extra year, and years they did not play were left out.

```{python}
# SQL only loads columns; all calculations and joins use Polars.
people = pl.read_database(
    "SELECT playerID, nameFirst, nameLast FROM people",
    con,
    infer_schema_length=None
)

appearances = pl.read_database(
    "SELECT playerID, yearID, G_all FROM appearances",
    con
)

# Career length means the number of seasons actually played.
# Count a year once, even if the player changed teams that year.
q1 = (
    appearances
    .filter(pl.col("G_all") > 0)
    .group_by("playerID")
    .agg(pl.col("yearID").n_unique().alias("career_length"))
    .join(people, on="playerID", how="inner")
    .rename({"nameFirst": "first_name", "nameLast": "last_name"})
    .select(["playerID", "first_name", "last_name", "career_length"])
    .sort(["career_length", "playerID"], descending=[True, False])
    .head(10)
)

q1
```

## QUESTION 2

First basemen had the highest average salary at about $3.35 million, while catchers had the lowest at about $1.44 million. I counted each player's yearly salary toward the position where they played the most games that year because it best represents their main role and keeps their salary from being counted twice. If two positions had the same number of games, I chose the position code that came first alphabetically.

```{python}
salaries = pl.read_database(
    "SELECT playerID, yearID, salary FROM salaries",
    con
)

fielding = pl.read_database(
    "SELECT playerID, yearID, POS, G FROM fielding",
    con
)

# Combine salary records from multiple teams into one total per player/year.
annual_salaries = (
    salaries
    .filter(pl.col("salary").is_not_null())
    .group_by(["playerID", "yearID"])
    .agg(pl.col("salary").sum().alias("salary"))
)

# Choose the position with the most games across all teams that year.
# This represents the player's main role and avoids counting salary twice.
# If games are tied, choose the first position alphabetically.
primary_positions = (
    fielding
    .group_by(["playerID", "yearID", "POS"])
    .agg(pl.col("G").sum().alias("games_at_position"))
    .sort(
        ["playerID", "yearID", "games_at_position", "POS"],
        descending=[False, False, True, False]
    )
    .unique(subset=["playerID", "yearID"], keep="first", maintain_order=True)
    .select(["playerID", "yearID", "POS"])
)

# Match salary to the position played in the same year.
# Player-years without a recorded fielding position are excluded.
salary_by_position = (
    annual_salaries
    .join(primary_positions, on=["playerID", "yearID"], how="inner")
)

# Average and maximum use annual salaries; total_players counts unique people.
# The salary data cover 1985-2016 and are not adjusted for inflation.
q2 = (
    salary_by_position
    .group_by("POS")
    .agg(
        pl.col("salary").mean().alias("average_salary"),
        pl.col("playerID").n_unique().alias("total_players"),
        pl.col("salary").max().alias("highest_salary")
    )
    .rename({"POS": "position"})
    .with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("average_salary") > 3_000_000)
        .then(pl.lit("High Salary"))
        .when(pl.col("average_salary") >= 2_000_000)
        .then(pl.lit("Medium Salary"))
        .otherwise(pl.lit("Low Salary"))
        .alias("salary_category"),
        pl.col("position").replace({
            "P": "Pitcher",
            "C": "Catcher",
            "1B": "First base",
            "2B": "Second base",
            "3B": "Third base",
            "SS": "Shortstop",
            "OF": "Outfielder"
        })
    )
    .sort("average_salary", descending=True)
    .with_columns(pl.col("average_salary").round(2))
)

con.close()
q2
```
